                                     PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                         § PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                      §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                   §            OF TEXAS


               COMMENTS OF PRIORITY POWER MANAGEMENT LLC
                     ON PROPOSED NEW 16 TAC §25.194

       COMES NOW Priority Power Management LLC (PPM or Priority Power) and files these

comments regarding the Commission’s proposed new 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC)

§25.194, relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards. The proposed rule would set forth the

standards and criteria for an electric utility to interconnect a large load customer to the ERCOT

transmission network. The Commission has requested that comments be filed by April 17, 2026,

and therefore these comments are timely filed.

                                      INTRODUCTION

       PPM is a North America energy services firm that supports large commercial, industrial,

and public-sector customers with powered land development, private energy infrastructure

solutions, microgrid and behind-the-meter solutions, energy procurement, and ongoing market and

operational management. Priority Power delivers generation- and load-side solutions for

customers – including mission-critical facilities – to ensure reliable power and enable long-term

growth.

       PPM appreciates the opportunity to file comments on the Commission’s proposed new

§25.194. Although PPM supports the Commission adopting a rule to provide market participants

with additional structure for this process, we continue to be concerned that the proposal shifts

significant capital risk to large load customers at too early a stage. Developing a rule that

establishes appropriate and necessary standards and processes for large load interconnection



                                Priority Power Comments on Proposed New 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 2
 requires a delicate balance. If the Commission fails to strike the right balance, the final rule will

have an adverse economic effect, chilling investment in Texas projects.


        COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC SUBSECTIONS OF THE PROPOSED RULE

Subsection (b), Applicability.

       Subsection (b) lays out several circumstances under which the new section would be

applicable to a large load customer that is seeking to interconnect to the system, including a new

interconnection of 75MW or more, an expanded interconnection that would equal 75MW or more

for the first time, or an expansion of an existing interconnection that would exceed 75MW by

75MW or more. Subparagraph (2) should be clarified so that it does not apply the full force of the

proposed rule to incremental additions of load that cause a customer’s total peak demand at a single

site to exceed 75 MW. In the case of midstream oil and gas facilities, there may be multiple meters

or distributed equipment where there is no individual component that has a peak demand that is

equal to or exceeds 75 MW, but as these components are installed over time and if they are netted,

they could equal or exceed that threshold. In these instances, the customer will not have requested

permission to interconnect the full 75 MW or more of load at the outset. PPM does not anticipate

that the Commission intends these gradually growing operations to be subject to the requirements

of the proposed rule. One potential solution to address this concern is to apply the rule to expanded

interconnections that cause the load to equal or exceed 75 MW within ten years of the customer’s

initial energization. This approach would recognize the slow growth of existing facilities without

inviting gamesmanship by new facilities seeking to avoid the application of the rule by initially

energizing at 74 MW and then expanding operations in the next few years.

       In addition, because there is the word “and” between subparagraphs (2) and (3), the rule

would apply to a large load customer only if it meets all three conditions. If the rule is intended to


                                 Priority Power Comments on Proposed New 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 3
 apply to a large load customer that meets any of the three conditions, the “and” should be changed

to “or.”

           Following are proposed language modifications to capture these recommendations:

(b)        Applicability. This section applies to a large load customer that seeks:
           (1)   a new interconnection that is equal to or exceeds 75 megawatts (MW);
           (2)   an expanded interconnection that would equals or exceeds 75 MW within 10 years
                 of the customer’s initial energization for the first time; or and
           (3)   an expanded interconnection that exceeds 75 MW by 75 MW or more.


Subsection (c), Definitions.

           Subsection (c)(9) defines Large Load Customer and measures the customer’s total peak

demand “at a single site.” As noted above, in the case of midstream oil and gas facilities, there

may be multiple meters or distributed equipment where there is no individual component that has

a peak demand that is equal to or exceeds 75 MW, but as these components are installed over time

and if they are netted, they could equal or exceed that threshold. In these instances, the customer

will not have requested permission to interconnect the full 75 MW or more of load at the outset.

PPM does not anticipate that the Commission intends these gradually growing operations to be

subject to the requirements of the proposed rule. To provide further clarity to the rule, the

Commission should clarify that a single site includes the load interconnected through the same

Facilities Extension Agreement (FEA). For example, this definition could be revised as follows:

           (9)    Large load customer -- A customer requesting a new or expanded
                  interconnection where the customer’s contracted total peak demand at a
                  single site that is interconnected to the electric grid through the same
                  facilities extension agreement and is reasonably forecast for interconnection
                  studies to equal to or exceed exceeds 75 megawatts (MW).

Subsection (d), Intermediate agreement.

           PPM continues to be concerned about excessive and duplicative financial security

requirements that must be posted by a large load customer. Paragraphs (d)(9)(A) and (B) require

                                   Priority Power Comments on Proposed New 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 4
 study fees of either $100,000 or $300,000, depending on the peak demand of the large load trying

to interconnect. It is not apparent that there is a cost-causation basis to increase the fee study fee

from $100,000 to $300,000 when a large load customer passes a base load of 250 MW. We note

that (d)(9)(D) requires that if the costs to conduct the interconnection study exceed the fee, then

the customer must pay the actual cost to conduct the study. As a result, a flat study fee of $100,000

would meet the requirements of Utilities Code §37.0561(f), and the provisions of subsection

(d)(9)(D) would ensure that the large load pays the actual cost of the fee to the extent it exceeds

$100,000. Accordingly, subsection (d)(9)(B) can be deleted.

       Paragraph (d)(10) requires financial security of $50,000 per megawatt of the requested

peak demand to be posted at the time of the intermediate agreement is executed. As an example, a

100 MW project would require $5,000,000 of security. PPM continues to object to the magnitude

of the security requirement of $50,000/MW because it is arbitrary and excessively high for this

point in development of a new project. Further, pursuant to later subsections of the rule, such as

subsections (g) and (h), if a large load withdraws its interconnection application after ERCOT

determines that inadequate capacity is available to the large load customer, only 20 percent of the

remaining amount is refundable after applying the financial security to outstanding amounts owed.

This 80% non-refundability is not cost-based and acts as a penalty, especially if ERCOT’s

subsequent analysis indicates that there is no, or economically insufficient, capacity available to

serve the proposed load. This structure should be modified. In the Commission’s Open Meeting

on March 12, 2026, Commissioners discussed the concept that financial security should be tied to

reasonable commercial development milestones. For example, Chairman Gleeson proposed that

if the security requirement were $50,000, then perhaps the initial payment would be $10,000 or

$20,000 and then would escalate as the project progresses through steps and becomes more



                                 Priority Power Comments on Proposed New 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 5
 commercially viable over time. Priority Power agrees that such an approach would be more

appropriate.

        Priority Power appreciates that one of the objectives to requiring this large posting of

financial security is to ensure that “real” large load customers are entering the batch study process,

but the magnitude of the amount of financial security coupled with the limited amount of

refundability will discourage the development of traditional industrial resources in the ERCOT

region. As a result, Priority Power recommends that the Commission increase the amount of the

posted financial security that is refundable, especially since all other costs ERCOT and the

interconnecting utilities may incur already will have been paid through the applicable study fee as

well as through the application of the financial security as well.

        As an alternative, PPM recommends instead that the penalty to the customer be a maximum

20 percent non-refundable security, although a lower amount of non-refundability would be more

appropriate. PPM will discuss this further in later subsections but raises the issue here as it relates

to the stacking of multiple payments that a large load customer must make under the proposed

rule.

        Finally, PPM recommends that the rule be clarified regarding how the utilities will handle

interest on cash collateral held as financial security pursuant to subsection (d)(10). The financial

security that would be required pursuant to this subsection does not appear to be within the scope

of existing 16 TAC §25.195, Terms and Conditions for Transmission Service, in which subsection

(e) requires in relevant part, “interest at a commercially reasonable rate based on that portion of

the deposit being returned.” As a result, this rule should specify the interest rate that will be paid

on security deposits made by large load customers, the process of accounting for interest should




                                  Priority Power Comments on Proposed New 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 6
 be transparent, and there should be clear requirements for the timely return of such collateral after

the costs that the collateral is securing payment of have been paid.

       PPM recommends the following modifications to subsection (d), consistent with our

recommendations above. We note that the published proposal is missing a paragraph (B), so the

following redlines include renumbered paragraphs:

       (10)    Financial security on a dollar per MW basis. An initial payment of 20 percent
               of the Ffinancial security under this subsection is due at the time that the
               intermediate agreement is executed, with the remaining amount paid on a ratable
               basis as commercial development milestones are achieved. A large load customer
               must post financial security with the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting
               TSP in the amount of $50,000 per MW of the requested peak demand for new
               interconnection requests or of the incremental increase in the peak demand for
               expanded interconnection requests.
               (A)     Beginning in 2027, the commission will adjust the $50,000 value on
                       January 1 every five years.
                       (i)     The annual adjustment will be proportional to the third quarter
                               percentage change in the national Consumer Price Index (CPI)
                               published by the United States Department of Labor, Bureau of
                               Labor Statistics.
                       (ii)    The executive director must designate a substitute index to be used
                               as a reference for adjustments if the CPI becomes unavailable.
               (BC) The interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP may accept the
                       following forms of financial security:
                       (i)     cash collateral;
                       (ii)    corporate or parental guaranty, only if the corporation or parent
                               corporation has a credit rating equivalent of BBB-/Baa3 or higher
                               from Standard & Poor’s or Moody’s; or
                       (iii)   a letter of credit issued by a major U.S. commercial bank, or a U.S.
                               branch office of a major foreign commercial bank, with a credit
                               rating of at least “A-” by Standard & Poor’s or “A3” by Moody’s
                               Investor Service.
               (CD) If the large load customer provides a corporate or parental guaranty under
                       this subsection, the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP may
                       require the submission of financial records or statements to determine the
                       customer’s financial stability.
               (DE) Refund of financial security posted on a dollar per MW basis is subject to
                       subsection (g) of this section, and, for cash collateral, must include interest
                       at a commercially-reasonable rate specified by the Commission.


                                 Priority Power Comments on Proposed New 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 7
 Subsection (f), Interconnection agreement.

       Priority Power notes that subsection (f)(7) requires a non-refundable interconnection fee

of $50,000/MW of contracted peak demand, thus adding to the list of fees discussed in subsection

(e) above. There does not appear to be a cost causation basis for this fee in light of other financial

security that a customer must post in order to proceed towards interconnection, including:

       1.   Financial security for significant equipment or services (subsection (f)(8));

       2. Contribution in Aid of Construction (CIAC) for all direct interconnection costs, with

            no standard or other allowance offered to offset the customer’s payment (subsection

            (f)(9)); and

       3. Financial security for system upgrades that are necessary to reliably serve the large load

            customer (subsection (f)(10)).

Priority Power appreciates that the Commission has clarified in (f)(7)(A) that any unused financial

security initially posted with the intermediate agreement would be drawn upon to satisfy the

interconnection fee requirement. But, in the event the interconnection fee is less than the amount

of the posted financial security, only 20% of the remaining balance would be refundable. PPM

further appreciates that the proposed rule would require the DSP or TSP to apply any unused study

fee paid under an intermediate agreement to satisfy financial security for significant equipment or

services, pursuant to (f)(8). These provisions reduce but do not eliminate PPM’s concerns about

stacking payments made by large load customers.

       Subsection (f)(9) requires payment of all direct interconnection costs via CIAC, without

any standard or allowance to offset the CIAC. The proposed CIAC requirements would benefit

from additional specificity. In particular, PPM strongly recommends that the Commission require

utilities to itemize costs for CIAC. This itemization is appropriate, given that the Commission is


                                 Priority Power Comments on Proposed New 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 8
 proposing to require a direct cash payment for CIAC under subparagraph (f)(9)(A). Further,

itemization would assist with the true-up process that is required by subparagraph (f)(9)(C).

       As proposed, subparagraph (f)(9)(A) requires CIAC to be paid in cash. While a cash-only

payment may be acceptable in many instances, since these rules are proposed to apply to any

industrial development with a capacity of 75 MW or more, PPM respectfully recommends the

Commission expand its range of acceptable forms of security to include surety bonds and other

commercially reasonable instruments that provide equivalent protection to utilities without

excluding otherwise viable projects. Some examples of other commercially reasonable forms of

security that could be used include project level escrow accounts, standby letters of credit with

broader issuer criteria, and affiliate guarantees. Paragraph (f)(9)(A) should be modified as follows:

       (A)     Direct interconnection costs include all costs associated with facilities built to
               interconnect the large load customer to the existing ERCOT system, including
               radial lines and substation upgrades necessary to interconnect the new large load
               customer. CIAC must be paid in the form of a direct cash payment, project level
               escrow accounts, standby letters of credit, or affiliate guarantees.


       Finally, PPM opposes the inclusion of paragraph (f)(10), which would require large load

customers to fund system upgrades that are remote from their point of direct interconnection to the

grid. While PPM agrees that it is appropriate for a large load customer to pay for their direct

interconnection costs, and to pay for increased transmission investment overall that ensures a

reliable grid with higher load, this paragraph would have individual customers funding upgrades

that benefit the system overall. This would be a significant departure from past policy wherein

transmission costs are socialized and could create a quagmire of issues related to establishing

priority access for certain users and diminishing access by lower priority users. As the rule is

structured, the non-refundable interconnection fee of $50,000 per MW of contracted demand

already serves as a contribution to cover the costs of increased investment in the transmission grid.

                                 Priority Power Comments on Proposed New 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 9
 In another proceeding, Project No. 58484, Evaluation of Transmission Cost Recovery, the

Commission will adopt rules that ensure a more equitable allocation of transmission costs is

recovered from all ERCOT consumers.           The combination of a significant non-refundable

interconnection fee and improved transmission cost recovery rules should achieve the broad

objective to ensure that residential customers do not bear the cost of transmission improvements

necessary to serve the rapid growth of large load customers. Priority Power urges the Commission

to stay true to the open access transmission policy with postage stamp access to the grid that has

served the competitive market well for more than 25 years. These policies have avoided

fundamental cost allocation logjams that have hindered growth in other energy markets in the

United States. For these reasons, PPM recommends that (f)(10) be deleted in its entirety as

follows:

       (10)    Financial security for system upgrades. A large load customer must post
               financial security for system upgrades that are necessary to reliably serve the large
               load customer not later than the date that the interconnection agreement is executed.
               (A)     The interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP may accept the
                       following forms of financial security for system upgrades:
                       (i)      cash collateral;
                       (ii)     corporate or parental guaranty, only if the corporation or parent
                                corporation has a credit rating equivalent of BBB-/Baa3 or higher
                                from Standard & Poor’s or Moody’s; or
                       (iii)    a letter of credit issued by a major U.S. commercial bank, or a U.S.
                                branch office of a major foreign commercial bank, with a credit
                                rating of at least “A-” by Standard & Poor’s or “A3” by Moody’s
                                Investor Service.
               (B)     If the large load customer provides a corporate or parental guaranty under
                       this subsection, the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP may
                       require the submission of financial records or statements to determine the
                       customer’s financial stability.
               (C)     Refund of financial security posted for system upgrades is subject to
                       subsections (g) through (i) of this section.




                               Priority Power Comments on Proposed New 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 10
 Subsection (g), Withdrawal of all or a portion of requested or contracted peak demand for
interconnection.

       Subsection (g)(3) allows that, after applying the financial security to outstanding amounts

owed, 80 percent of the remaining amount of financial security is non-refundable. The remaining

80 percent of the balance would be applied as an offset to the interconnecting utility’s rate base

pursuant to (g)(4). This structure is weighed unreasonably against the large load customer and

should be modified. As discussed previously, the Commissioners discussed at their Open Meeting

on March 12, 2026, the concept of tying financial security to the achievement of reasonable

commercial development milestones. For example, Chairman Gleeson proposed that if the

security requirement were $50,000 per MW, then perhaps the initial payment would be $10,000

per MW or $20,000 per MW and then would escalate and become less refundable as the project

progresses through steps and becomes more commercially viable over time. Priority Power agrees

that such an approach would be more appropriate. As an alternative, PPM recommends instead

that the penalty to the customer be 20 percent non-refundable security. Chairman Gleeson indicated

during the Open Meeting his preference that any remaining non-refundable security should be

applied to rates, not “rate base,” and this clarification is included in proposed redlines below.

       Additionally, Priority Power opposes paragraph (g)(5), stating that CIAC is not refundable.

In subsection (f)(9)(C), a large load customer that interconnects to the grid is allowed to receive a

credit on their bill for the difference in actual costs relative to the estimate. This same approach

should be used in the event that a large load customer does not interconnect with the grid – the

large load customer should receive a refund to the extent the amount paid exceeds the actual costs

incurred.

       Paragraph (g) should be modified as follows:




                                Priority Power Comments on Proposed New 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 11
 (g)    Withdrawal of all or a portion of requested peak demand or contracted peak demand.
       A large load customer may withdraw all or a portion of its requested peak demand or
       contracted peak demand for interconnection by submitting its request in writing to the
       interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP.
       (1)    Not later than 14 days after receipt of a large load customer’s notice to withdraw
              all or a portion of requested peak demand or contracted peak demand for
              interconnection, the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP must notify
              ERCOT via a method prescribed by ERCOT.
       (2)    The interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP must draw down on the large
              load customer’s financial security and apply the financial security to any
              outstanding amounts owed. Outstanding amounts owed include the following:
              (A)      costs incurred by the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP to
                       fulfill the large load customer’s request for interconnection;
              (B)      costs for equipment that the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP
                       procured and that cannot be canceled with a full refund;
              (C)      costs for construction that the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting
                       TSP started and that cannot be canceled with a full refund; and
              (D)      costs for services that the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP
                       initiated and that cannot be canceled with a full refund.
       (3)    After applying the large load customer’s financial security to any outstanding
              amounts owed, the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP must refund
              820% of the balance to the large load customer within 60 days.
       (4)    After applying the financial security to any outstanding amounts owed and
              refunding 820% of the balance, the remaining 280% of the balance must be paid to
              the interconnecting TSP and applied by that TSP as an offset to the interconnecting
              TSP’s rates base in the earlier of the interconnecting TSP’s next interim rate
              proceeding or comprehensive rate proceeding.
       (5)    If CIAC paid exceeds the actual costs incurred, the excess CIAC paid is not
              refundable.
       (6)    ERCOT must reallocate contracted peak demand that is withdrawn by a large load
              customer.

Subsection (h), Non-utilized capacity.

       Subsection (h) establishes a process whereby an interconnecting TSP or DSP must notify

ERCOT if a large load customer fails to satisfy, by six months, a milestone in its schedule for

phased energization. The subsection further requires a draw down on financial security, partial

refund, and reallocation of non-utilized capacity. Although it may seem logical to link this time

frame to time frames being used in the ERCOT batch process, six months is an unreasonably short


                               Priority Power Comments on Proposed New 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 12
 time frame for eliminating a project, given the substantial supply chain limitations faced in the

market at this time and many other factors that can cause unforeseen delays. PPM recommends

modifying the six-month milestone to accommodate supply chain limitations or other

contingencies that are specifically out of the customer's control, such as transformer failures, in

which transformers have a 24–36-month (or longer) replacement cycle, non-transformer supply

chain delays, or other engineering, procurement, and construction delays outside a large load

customer's control. At a minimum, PPM recommends that the proposed six-month period be

subject to an extension for good cause shown. However, due to the significant supply chain issues

that the electric industry is facing at this time, PPM recommends increasing to a 48-month window,

plus the opportunity to request a good cause exception for events not tied to over-requesting

capacity.

       As an alternative, in the context of Project No. 58484, relating to Evaluation of

Transmission Cost Recovery, one approach to reforming transmission cost recovery is to institute

a take-or-pay concept1 whereby a large load customer is required to pay for capacity they request

(and are granted) to interconnect to the grid for a set period of time, such as 10 years. The end of

this mandated period of the take-or-pay construct could be an alternative time at which the large

load customer could relinquish capacity that will not be needed for future operations.

       Similarly to subsection (g) discussed above, subsection (h)(3) and (4) would allow only 20

percent of any remaining financial security to be refunded to the large load customer, with the

remaining 80 percent being applied as an offset to rate base. Again, this structure is weighed

unreasonably against the large load customer and should be modified so that the non-refundable




1
 See Project No. 58484, Oncor Electric Delivery’s Comments on Commission Staff’s Draft Set of
Recommendations (Apr. 13, 2026) at 1.

                                Priority Power Comments on Proposed New 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 13
 penalty to the customer is 20 percent rather than 80 percent. For consistency, subsection (h) should

be modified similarly to mirror subsection (g).

       Finally, subsection (h)(5) states that CIAC is not refundable. However, if ERCOT

reallocates that customer’s capacity to a subsequent large load customer, and equipment or services

that the original customer paid for through CIAC are used to support the interconnection of the

subsequent customer, then subsequent customer should be charged CIAC to pay for the upgrades

that they are now using for themselves, and the original customer should receive a refund from the

electric utility for the cost of that equipment or services. At a minimum, the language should be

modified to allow for a refund to a large load customer within 60 days if the capacity is reassigned

to another customer. Additionally, we recommend that the Commission clarify that CIAC is

refundable to the extent the amount paid exceeds the actual costs incurred. Paragraph (f)(9)(C)

allows for refund of financial security posted for system upgrades and given that refunds are

allowed under those circumstances, it is appropriate to allow for refunds for withdrawal of all or a

portion of requested or contracted peak demand for interconnection.

       Consistent with PPM’s recommendations above, subsection (h) should be modified as

follows:

(h)    Non-utilized capacity.

       (1)     For good cause shown, the interconnecting DSP or TSP must extend the time for a
               large load customer to satisfy a milestone in its schedule for phased energization to
               account for contingencies that are out of the large load customer's control. Not later
               than 30 days after a large load customer fails, by 6 48 months, to satisfy a milestone
               in its schedule for phased energization, the interconnecting DSP or the
               interconnecting TSP must notify ERCOT of the large load customer’s non-utilized
               capacity.
       (2)     Within 60 days of providing notice to ERCOT under this subsection, the
               interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP must draw down on the large load
               customer’s financial security and apply the financial security to any outstanding
               amounts owed. Outstanding amounts owed include the following:


                                Priority Power Comments on Proposed New 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 14
                (A)     costs incurred by the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP to
                       fulfill the large load customer’s request for interconnection;
               (B)     costs for equipment that the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP
                       procured and that cannot be canceled with a full refund;
               (C)     costs for construction that the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting
                       TSP started and that cannot be canceled with a full refund; and
               (D)     costs for services that the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP
                       initiated and that cannot be canceled with a full refund.
       (3)     Within 60 days of providing notice to ERCOT under this subsection and after
               applying the large load customer’s financial security to any outstanding amounts
               owed, the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP must refund 820% of
               the balance to the large load customer.
       (4)     After applying the financial security to any outstanding amounts owed and
               refunding 820% of the balance, the remaining 280% of the balance must be paid to
               the interconnecting TSP and applied by that TSP as an offset to the interconnecting
               TSP’s rates base in the earlier of the interconnecting TSP’s next interim rate
               proceeding or comprehensive rate proceeding.
       (5)     If CIAC paid exceeds the actual costs incurred, the excess CIAC paid is not
               refundable. If some or all of the capacity is reassigned to one or more other
               customers, CIAC paid that is attributable to equipment and services reassigned to
               one or more customers must be refunded within 60 days of such reassignment.
       (6)     ERCOT must reallocate non-utilized capacity.

In the event the Commission adopts a take-or-pay construct for transmission cost recovery from

large load customers, alternate revisions to subjection (h) would be required.

Subsection (i), Terms for refund of financial security for a large load customer that energizes.

       Subsection (i) provides for a process to refund financial security to a customer that

energizes. Paragraph (i)(1) would first apply amounts owed and then refund 20 percent of the

balance remaining after the large load energizes, and then ratably as the large load meets the

milestones in the customer’s schedule for phased energization of its contracted peak demand.

Paragraph (i)(2) states that any remaining balance would be refunded when the large load customer

sustains operations for five years at the customer’s contracted peak demand. Additional clarity is

needed, because if (i)(1) requires a ratable (pro-rata) refund as they meet the milestones, then that

would suggest that the remainder would be refunded once the customer has reached full


                                Priority Power Comments on Proposed New 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 15
 energization capacity. Some flexibility should be incorporated to account for the very likely

circumstance that a customer cannot operate precisely at their original projected peak demand

because of unforeseen issues precluding full use of that capacity. For this reason, we recommend

that the remaining balance be refunded when the large load operates for at least 95% of contracted

peak demand for at least one year. At this point, the large load customer will have paid

$50,000/MW as a non-refundable interconnection fee, paid their CIAC, paid for significant

equipment and services, and will be paying their cost of transmission pursuant to new rules the

Commission will adopt in Project No. 58484. It is unclear what public policy is served through

continued delay of refunding financial security at this point.

       Consistent with these recommendations, PPM recommends modifications of subsection (i)

as follows:

(i)    Terms for refund of financial security for a large load customer that energizes. An
       interconnecting DSP or an interconnecting TSP must draw down on the large load
       customer’s financial security and apply the financial security to any outstanding amounts
       owed for costs incurred by the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP to fulfill
       the large load customer’s request for interconnection of the contracted peak demand.
